title: Alpine pastures: grazing below the natural tree line
place: Alps and Prealps around the tree line (about 1800–2400 m); example Davos, Dischma valley (GR)
built: from prehistory and the Middle Ages; retreat since the 1970s
summary: For many centuries herders cleared forest to enlarge the summer pastures of the Alps and pushed the tree line down; since the 1970s many pastures are no longer used and forest grows back.
why: In summer, farmers take their cattle up to the alpine pastures (Alpen). The grass in the valley can then be cut for winter hay. Pollen studies show how the forest changed. The Historical Dictionary of Switzerland (HLS) says that alpine grazing was possibly linked to a lowering of the tree line by clearing. In the Middle Ages more cattle farming led to a slow spread of treeless high pastures, and the upper tree line went down.

In Switzerland the tree line is at about 2000 m today. Alpine pastures and meadows lie mainly between 1800 and 2400 m. Where cattle graze, the forest cannot come back; grazing also kept many larch forests open.

After the 1970s, less land was farmed in the traditional way, and the forest advanced. Between 1985 and 2018 the alpine pasture area fell by 401 km² (7 %). New forest and woods grew on 280 km² of former alpine pastures. Above 2000 m the wooded area grew by a third or more, also because the climate is warmer.
gained: Summer grass for cattle. A study of 2012 says that more fodder for the home farm is the main reason to send animals to the alpine pastures.
Wide open high pastures above the forest. In the Middle Ages more cattle farming slowly widened these treeless pastures.
lost: Mountain forest: the upper tree line went down in the Middle Ages. A higher tree line can protect against avalanches, says a WSL researcher quoted by SRF.
Today the opposite happens. New forest grew on 280 km² of former alpine pastures between 1985 and 2018, and plant and animal communities shaped by farming disappear.

stops.title: Pastures above Davos
text: The map of 1880 shows the Davos area. Above the forest lie the alpine pastures. People made many of them by clearing forest over many centuries.
There is no line on this map: the old forest edge before the clearings is not known.

stops.title: Forest comes back
text: Today fewer pastures are used than in the 19th century. In the Dischma valley spruce grows up into larch forests that grazing once kept open.
Across Switzerland, new forest grew on 280 km² of former alpine pastures between 1985 and 2018.

notes: No shape is drawn. The natural tree line before the clearings cannot be read from any map (the oldest maps are from 1844, long after the clearings), and no source gives a mapped former forest edge for a sample area. A sample comparison of forest edges 1880/today would show forest regrowth, which belongs to the forest changes. Facts: HLS Wald (lowering of the tree line by clearing linked with alpine grazing, possibly prehistoric; medieval spread of treeless high pastures; forest advance after the 1970s; pollen analyses); BFS Land use in Switzerland 2018 (published 2021): tree line at about 2000 m, alpine pastures 1800-2400 m, alpine agricultural area -401 km2 (-7 %) 1985-2018, new wooded areas on 280 km2 of former alpine agricultural area, above 2000 m wooded area +1/3 or more, climate as a further cause; SRF 29 July 2023 (Davos, Dischma, Stillberg; tree line rising also because fewer alpine pastures are used than in the 19th century; spruce into larch forests once kept open by grazing; avalanche protection); WSL waldwissen 2008 (5800 ha more forest in potential avalanche release zones above 1200 m). The places Davos, Dischma and Stillberg were located with OpenStreetMap Nominatim. The often-quoted lowering of the tree line by 200-300 m was NOT found in a source and is not used. HLS gives natural tree-line changes of 100-300 m caused by climate after the Preboreal; this is not the human lowering.

title: Lavaux vineyard terraces
place: Steep north shore of Lake Geneva between Lutry and Vevey; sample area Dézaley and Epesses
summary: From the 12th century monks cleared the steep slope above Lake Geneva and planted vines; later generations built about 10,000 terraces held by about 450 km of walls.
why: The slope of Lavaux is very steep and faces south over Lake Geneva. In 1141 and 1142 the bishop of Lausanne gave land at Dézaley to two Cistercian monasteries (religious houses of monks), Hautcrêt and Montheron. The monks cleared the slope and planted vines. They owned the land until 1536.

To work the steep ground, people built walls and terraces (flat steps of soil held by a wall). At Dézaley the terraces date from the 18th century to 1839. Today Lavaux has about 10,000 terraces and about 450 km of walls on about 900 hectares.

In the 20th century Vaud protected the landscape. In 1977 the voters put an article that protects Lavaux into the cantonal constitution. A law on the protection plan of Lavaux came into force in 1979. In 2007 UNESCO listed Lavaux as a World Heritage cultural landscape (a landscape shaped by people).
gained: The terraces made it possible to grow vines on a slope that is too steep for normal fields. Chasselas grapes cover more than 60 % of the terraced vineyard today.
In 2007 UNESCO listed Lavaux as a 'thriving cultural landscape'. UNESCO says that its wine was a significant part of the local economy.
lost: The walls need constant work. After the very heavy rain of 2021 and the heat and drought of 2022–2023, many walls fell because the soil moved.

title: Sihlwald: from Zurich's wood supply to wilderness
place: Sihlwald forest on the left bank of the Sihl, between Langnau am Albis and Sihlbrugg
built: Used for wood from about 1300; no cutting since 2000
summary: For about 700 years the city of Zurich used the Sihlwald for firewood and timber; since 2000 nobody cuts trees there and the beech forest is returning to wilderness.
why: From about 1300 the city of Zurich took over the Sihlwald on the left bank of the Sihl. Wood was the main fuel of the city. Logs were floated down the Sihl to Zurich. From the late Middle Ages until 1856 the city held the right to float wood on the Sihl.

Zurich managed the forest closely. A forest law of 1483 reduced the old use rights of farmers. From 1601 there were heavy fines for damage and illegal wood sales. In the 19th century forestry became sustainable (only as much wood is cut as grows). Rafting ended in 1864. A workshop in the forest employed about 100 people, and a forest railway was built in 1876.

From 1986 a project planned to let the forest grow wild. The workshop closed in 1991. In 2000 all forest work stopped. The forest reserve came into force in 2008, and since 2010 the Sihlwald is a nature discovery park of national importance.
gained: About 970 ha of mixed beech forest can now develop without cutting. Rare species, old trees and fungi live there.
In 2008 the voters of the city of Zurich approved the Wildnispark Zurich with 89.6% yes.
lost: Since 2000 no wood is cut in the Sihlwald. From about 1300 the city had used its timber for building, trade and firewood.
The workshop in the Sihlwald, with about 100 workers in the 19th century, closed in 1991. Polluted ground from the workshop had to be cleaned in 1995.

stops.title: A working forest for the city
text: In 1880 the Sihlwald was a working forest of the city of Zurich. Wood went to the city by road and, until 1864, by floating on the Sihl.
The forest had a workshop and its own forest railway.

stops.title: A forest left to itself
text: Since 2000 nobody cuts trees in the Sihlwald. Dead trees stay in the forest.
The forest area did not change much. What changed is the use: from wood production to wilderness.

notes: Timeline from the Wildnispark Zürich history page (park operator, interested party). The right to float wood until 1856 is from HLS 'Sihl'; the park page gives 1864 as the 'end of timber rafting'. Both are given in the text (right vs. practice); the difference is not resolved. Area 970 ha and species statement from the park page. No shapes: the forest area of the Sihlwald did not change much; the change is in use, not in extent. 'The forest area did not change much' is based on a look at the maps of 1880 and today, not on a measured comparison. 'Dead trees stay in the forest' follows from the end of forest work (park page); no deadwood numbers were found.

title: Bannwald of Andermatt
place: Slope of the Gurschen above the village of Andermatt, Urseren valley
built: Protected since 1397; reforested from the 19th century
summary: A small protected forest above Andermatt has held back avalanches since at least 1397; from the 19th century it was enlarged by planting.
why: The Urseren valley lost most of its forest early. The study of the forest names a colder climate, more people, traffic over the passes and constant grazing as causes. Young trees could not grow. Around 200 years ago the forest above Andermatt, about 4 ha, was the last piece of the old forest in the valley.

The forest protects the village from avalanches. A ban letter (Bannbrief, a written order that forbids the use of a forest) of 1397 protected it. People were not allowed to take living or dead wood, cones or leaves from it.

After large avalanche accidents, people began to plant trees around the old core. The work began about 1850 and was combined with avalanche barriers on the upper slope. By 1950 the Bannwald had doubled in size. In the whole valley, forest grew from 4.4 ha in 1879 to 72.4 ha in 1950. After the avalanche winters of 1951/52 and 1974/75 more planting and barriers followed.
gained: The Bannwald has protected people and buildings in Andermatt from avalanches for centuries.
Forest in the Urseren valley grew from 4.4 ha in 1879 to 72.4 ha in 1950. In 1995 the forest office counted about 160 ha in the valley, including open and unproductive parts.
lost: The ban took the forest away from local use. People could not collect wood, cones or leaves there.
The planters used almost only spruce. Larch and Swiss stone pine mostly died, and trees from unsuitable origins grew badly. Large parts of the planted forest are in poor condition today.

title: Wood for the Bex salt works (Trient valley)
place: Salt works of Roche and Bex (VD); forests bought in the Trient valley near Salvan and Martigny (VS)
summary: The salt works of Bex burned huge amounts of wood; when the nearby forests were used up, Bern bought forests in the Trient valley, and their clearing caused floods and debris flows at Salvan.
why: For centuries Switzerland had to import most of its salt. At Bex people found salt springs, and from 1582 salt works boiled the salt water (brine) over wood fires. To get one tonne of salt they needed about one and a half tonnes of wood. In the 18th century the salt works made 1,000 to 1,500 tonnes of salt per year.

The forests near the salt works were soon used up. Wood was brought by floating it down the rivers; in 1695 an arch dam was built at the Joux-Verte to float wood to Roche. In 1705 the salt works bought wood from Martigny in the Trient valley. In 1706 the commune of Salvan sold a forest to the director of the salt works for 50 years of cutting.

The cuts had severe effects. According to a complaint of 1733, the soil became unstable. Rain washed earth and stones into the valley. In 1732 and 1733 the Trient broke its dyke and flooded farmland. In 1734 the salt works promised to pay 100 écus (silver coins) in compensation. Later, coal and then electricity (1943) replaced wood at Bex.
gained: The salt works gave Bern and later Vaud their own salt. Today the Saline de Bex still produces about 35,000 tonnes per year.
The communes earned money from their forests. Martigny sold its wood in the Trient valley for 50 pistoles (gold coins), and Salvan sold a forest for 18 pistoles.
lost: The forests near the salt works were soon used up, and forests in the Trient valley were cut. The people of Salvan feared a lack of wood in their valley.
Without forest, rockfall and debris reached the Trient. In 1732 and 1733 floods destroyed the dyke and damaged farmland. The work of the woodcutters became more dangerous.
Cuts on Martigny land on the other side of the valley destroyed young trees, and so pasture was lost.

stops.title: Salt works that burned forests

text: After the cuts the slopes above the Trient became unstable. Rain carried earth and stones down.

title: Peat cutting in the raised bogs (sample: Les Ponts-de-Martel)
place: Raised bogs of the Mittelland and the Jura; sample area the valley of La Sagne and Les Ponts-de-Martel (NE)
built: early 18th century – 1987 (peak in the second half of the 19th century and in both world wars)
summary: From the 18th century people cut peat as fuel in almost all raised bogs of the Mittelland and the Jura; the Rothenthurm initiative of 1987 ended it.
why: Peat is the brown soil of a raised bog (a bog fed only by rain), made of plants that did not rot. Dried, it burns. In Switzerland peat was first used as fuel at the start of the 18th century, in Zurich and Neuchâtel. People cut it by hand and dried the blocks in the air. It replaced firewood when wood was short.

The second half of the 19th century was the 'golden age' of peat cutting, with more people and industry. Almost all raised bogs of the Mittelland and the Jura were cut. Imported coal later replaced most peat, but in both world wars coal was rationed and peat was cut again on a large scale. After 1945 peat was used mainly in gardens.

In 1987 the Swiss voters accepted the Rothenthurm initiative. It protects the moors and bans peat cutting. The valley of Les Ponts-de-Martel still has the largest raised bogs of Switzerland, about 130 hectares; most of them show traces of peat cutting. In 2010 members of parliament and Pro Natura asked for a stop of peat imports, which were estimated at 150,000 tonnes per year.
gained: Fuel, mostly for heating. When coal was rationed in the two world wars, peat was cut on a large scale again.
Farmland: at Les Ponts-de-Martel, fairly intensive crops now grow on former bogs.
lost: Most raised bogs lost much of their peat, which took thousands of years to grow. At Les Ponts-de-Martel long peat mounds covered with meadows show how large the bogs once were.
Habitats of wet land. The remaining bogs are very important for many insects, birds and reptiles. In some old peat pits, bog plants slowly come back.

stops.title: A valley of bogs
text: The map shows the wide, flat valley of Les Ponts-de-Martel with its marsh symbols. The whole valley floor was once a marsh.
People cut peat here for fuel, also in both world wars.

stops.title: Bogs, meadows and peat mounds
text: Today the remaining bogs form a patchwork with meadows and fields. Bare peat and old peat pits are still visible. Since 1987 peat cutting is banned.
The site is a moorland of national importance.

notes: No shape is drawn. On the map of 1880 this area shows the old Dufour-type sheet with scattered marsh symbols; the edges of the bogs and of the cut areas cannot be traced reliably, and the bogs themselves belong to the marsh changes. title: Federal forest police laws of 1876 and 1902
place: All of Switzerland (1876: the Alps and Prealps; from 1902: the whole country)
summary: After the floods of 1868 the federal government took control of mountain forests in 1876 and of all forests from 1902; clearing was forbidden and new protection forests were planted.
why: Until the 19th century wood was almost the only fuel and raw material. Households, industries such as iron works, glass works and salt works, and farmers with their animals used the forest heavily. In the first half of the 19th century forest area went down. Forests were cut without new planting and the land was then used for farming.

From the middle of the 19th century foresters and hydrologists (scientists of water) linked the floods to the overuse of mountain forests. Reports for the federal government by Elias Landolt (1862) on mountain forests and by Carl Culmann (1864) on mountain torrents showed the damage. The floods of 1868 in Uri, St. Gallen, Graubünden, Valais and Ticino killed more than 50 people.

The constitution of 1874 gave the federal government the control of forest and water police in the high mountains. The law of 24 March 1876 forbade the reduction of forest area. It also asked for new protection forests where planting could give protection. In 1897 the limit 'in the high mountains' was removed. A new law of 1902, in force from 1903, protected the forest area in all of Switzerland. The Forest Act of 1991 replaced it.
gained: In the 20th century forest area in Switzerland grew by more than 40%, mainly because of planting, to 12,340 km2 in 1995. That is about 30% of the country.
Large reforestation projects were carried out along the whole Prealps from Lake Constance to Lake Geneva, mainly on slopes in danger of erosion.
Today about one third of Switzerland is forest. 44% of the forest protects people and infrastructure from natural hazards such as rockfall and avalanches.
lost: Many cantons resisted, because they had to build forest services and accept federal rules.
The law pushed farming out of the forest. Forest grazing and other traditional uses were stopped, and owners of new protection forests lost pasture land.
The ban on clearing did not stop all clearing. During the Second World War, more than 100 km2 of forest were cleared for fields.

stops.title: Floods and overused forests

stops.title: The first federal forest law
text: On 24 March 1876 the federal parliament passed the forest police law for the high mountains. It forbade the reduction of forest and asked for new protection forests.

stops.title: More forest than 150 years ago

Schuler) and HLS 'Forstgesetze'; BAFU page '150 Jahre Forstpolizeigesetz' (1868 floods, >50 deaths, one third forest, 44% protection forest from Waldbericht 2025). title: Reforestation of the Senseoberland
place: Upper Sense valleys (Plasselbschlund, Schwarzseeschlund, Muscherenschlund) south of Plasselb and Plaffeien
summary: From 1890 the canton of Fribourg bought about 1,800 ha of pasture in the Senseoberland and planted about 1,500 ha with forest to stop floods and erosion.
why: The Senseoberland is a steep area of soft flysch rock (layers of clay and sandstone that slide easily). People cleared much forest there from the 11th to the 14th century for sheep pasture. In the 19th century, large cuts for industry and export followed. By about 1875 only about 10% of the land had forest. Floods, erosion and a lack of wood hit the poor region hard.

The federal forest police law of 1876 included this part of Fribourg in the federal forest zone. The law allowed federal money for new protection forests. Fribourg waited, but in 1889 the federal government pushed the canton to act. In May 1890 the federal government agreed to pay 60% of the costs. On 19 November 1890 the Grand Council decided to buy three pastures and plant them. They lay in the catchments of the Höllbach and the Gerine (Ärgera).

From 1890 to 1914 the canton bought about 700 ha and planned 430 ha of new forest. Workers drained the wet soil, planted trees, built check dams (small walls across a stream that hold back gravel), fences and paths. The work went on after 1914. In the three valleys about 1,500 ha of former pasture became forest. The sample square on the map shows part of the Höllbach and Gerine catchment.
gained: A study of the project says that the main aims of 1890 were reached. The force of the streams was broken and erosion was stopped.
The lack of wood of the 19th century turned into a surplus of wood.
In the sample square, forest covered about 114 ha (34%) on the Siegfried map of 1890 and about 226 ha (68%) in OpenStreetMap today (measured on the maps).
lost: The canton bought about 1,800 ha of land and planted forest on about 1,500 ha of it. This land is no longer pasture.
The same study says that land use is still not ideal in every respect. Farmers, nature protection groups and others now have new demands on the forest.

title: Forest returns to Ticino's mountain slopes (Valle Onsernone)
place: Canton of Ticino; example Valle Onsernone west of Locarno
summary: When mountain farming ended, forest spread over Ticino's pastures and meadows: from about 60,000 ha (20%) around 1900 to about 140,000 ha (50%) around 2000.
why: For centuries people in the Ticino valleys used every slope. They kept animals on meadows and pastures and cut wood. In the Valle Onsernone the poor land allowed only some grazing, so people also worked with wood and made straw hats. The valley had 3,470 people in 1870.

In the 20th century people left the mountains. In Ticino, 45.5% of workers were in farming and forestry in 1900, but only 1.6% in 2000. The population of the Onsernone fell to 994 in 1970 and 852 in 2000. Nobody cut the meadows or grazed the pastures any more.

Trees grew on the abandoned land. Forest in Ticino grew from about 60,000 ha around 1900 to about 85,000 ha in 1950 and about 140,000 ha around 2000. From 1983/85 to 2009/17 it grew by another 16%, mostly above 800 m. Below 600 m, mainly in the plains and valley floors, forest area went down.
gained: The canton's forest plan says that the spread of forest on mountain slopes improves the safety of the land. 66,600 ha of forest now protect settlements and roads directly from natural hazards.
In 2002 the Onsernone forest reserve was created, mainly with silver fir. After the national park it is the largest nature protection area in Switzerland.
lost: The old mix of forest and open land disappears. The forest plan says this mix is part of the traditional landscape and attracts tourists. Forest interests must therefore be balanced with farming and nature protection.
Ticino has the most forest fires in Switzerland: 820 of 2,473 Swiss forest fires from 2000 to 2022. The fire risk tends to increase.
Much of the wood stays in the forest. In 2022 about 111,100 m3 were cut, about one fifth of the usable amount. One reason is the high cost of cutting and bringing the wood out.

title: The 'Anbauschlacht': more fields in the Second World War (sample: Kühwald)
place: Whole of Switzerland; sample area Kühwald near Dürrenroth (Emmental, BE)
summary: To feed the country during the Second World War, Switzerland almost doubled its cropland from 183,000 to 352,000 hectares and cleared about 12,900 hectares of forest.
why: Before the Second World War Switzerland imported much of its food. When the war cut imports, there was a risk of hunger. In 1939 and 1940 the Federal Council ordered more cropland. On 15 November 1940 Friedrich Traugott Wahlen presented a larger plan, the 'Plan Wahlen'. Its aim was about 500,000 hectares of crops, so that the country could live without imports.

Farmers turned meadows into fields. Marshes were drained and fields were joined (land improvement). Between 1941 and 1946 as much land was drained and joined as in the 50 years before. Forest was cleared for fields: in total 12,902 hectares between 1940 and November 1946. Even city squares became fields, for example the Sechseläutenplatz in Zurich in 1942.

The sample area is the Kühwald near Dürrenroth in the Emmental, a conifer forest of 6 hectares. It was cleared as part of the land improvement of the Waltrigenmoos (1943–1951). The maps show the forest in 1940 and fields in 1960.
gained: Cropland grew from 183,000 hectares to 352,000 hectares by 1945. Self-sufficiency (the share of food grown in the country) rose from 52 % to 59 %.
According to the HLS, the plan was a long-term strategy to modernise farming, and it worked far beyond the war.
lost: About 12,900 hectares of forest were cleared. The law asked for new forest elsewhere as a replacement; after the war this was done partly in the mountains.
Large areas of wet land were drained: from 1941 to 1946 as much land was drained and joined as in the 50 years before.
Even so, the average food per person fell from about 3,200 to 2,200 calories per day.

title: Wartime forest clearing at Junzlen (Meiringen)
place: Junzlen, valley floor of the Aare west of Meiringen; example of the clearings of 1941-1946 in all of Switzerland
summary: During the Second World War Switzerland cleared about 12,900 ha of forest and scrub for farmland; at Junzlen near Meiringen a 26 ha forest on the Aare plain was cleared in 1943.
why: During the Second World War food was short. The 'Anbauschlacht' (the plan to grow much more food in Switzerland) needed new fields. On 21 March 1941 a federal order obliged the cantons to clear 2,000 ha of forest at first. In 1942 the target rose by another 10,000 ha. Canton Bern had to clear 3,400 ha.

The Bern forest office wanted to clear forests on river floodplains, because their wood had little value and their soil seemed good for fields. One of them was the Junzlen on the Aare west of Meiringen. It was a 26 ha coppice forest (low forest that people cut often for firewood). It was the only floodplain forest on the first list that was really cleared, in 1943.

From 1940 to November 1946 about 12,902 ha were cleared in Switzerland. 9,137 ha of it was real forest, the rest was scrub. The forest law stayed in force, so each clearing needed a permit. A federal decree of 20 December 1946 asked for new forest in the mountains as a replacement. By 1962 only 8,700 ha had been planted.
gained: The clearings gave new land for food production in a time of shortage. The cultivated area of Switzerland (Anbaufläche) reached its maximum of 367,048 ha in 1945. The plan had aimed at more than 500,000 ha.
At Junzlen the valley floor became farmland. On the swisstopo maps of 1960 and today, open fields lie where the forest stood (seen on the maps).
lost: About 9,100 ha of real forest and 3,800 ha of scrub were lost in Switzerland. The forest was also overused by larger cuts during the war.
The study of the clearings found that floodplain soils did not always give good fields. Some cleared areas were later built over, for example in Bätterkinden, Burgdorf and Kirchberg.
At Junzlen only small strips of forest remain: about 2 ha in OpenStreetMap today, against about 24 ha on the map of 1938 (measured on the maps).

title: Towns grow over farmland (sample: west of Lausanne)
place: Whole of Switzerland; sample area Ecublens, Chavannes-près-Renens and Renens west of Lausanne
built: mainly since 1950; sample area: strongest growth from the 1960s
summary: Between 1985 and 2018 the settlement area of Switzerland grew by 776 km² (31 %), nine tenths of it on former farmland; west of Lausanne small farming villages became one town.
why: Switzerland has more people, and each person uses more space for living, work and transport. Between 1985 and 2018 the settlement area (buildings, roads, gardens, parks, railways) grew by 776 km², or 31 %. Nine tenths of the new settlement area was built on former farmland. About one square metre of farmland disappears every second.

The sample area is west of Lausanne. Ecublens, Chavannes and Renens were farming and wine villages. In 1850 they had together about 1,100 people. A railway yard came to Renens in 1876. From the 1960s, with the motorway (1964) and new firms, the villages grew very fast. The University of Lausanne came to Dorigny in 1970 and the EPFL (federal institute of technology) in 1977. In 2000 the three communes had about 34,700 people.

Growth has slowed. Settlement area grew by about 27 km² per year in 1985–1997 and by about 20 km² per year in 2009–2018. Since 2014 a revised federal planning law asks for smaller building zones and denser towns, to stop urban sprawl and protect farmland.
gained: Homes, jobs and schools for a growing population with higher needs for living space, leisure and transport.
In Ecublens the University of Lausanne (1970) and the EPFL (1977) settled at Dorigny. They use one fifth of the commune. Several large firms also came.
lost: Farmland: between 1985 and 2018 Switzerland lost 1,097 km² of agricultural land (7 %). In the Mittelland most of it was built on.

Fields, orchards and vines between the villages. In the sample box the village cores of 1880 covered about 18 hectares; today the built-up area is about 640 hectares (measured on the maps, method see notes).

title: The loss of tall fruit-tree orchards (sample: Roggwil TG)
place: Whole of Switzerland; sample area Böler near Roggwil in the Thurgau fruit region
summary: Around 1950 Switzerland had about 15 million tall fruit trees (Hochstamm); state felling campaigns (1950–1975) and modern farming cut this to about 2.2 million.
why: Tall fruit trees (Hochstamm: apple, pear and cherry trees with a high trunk) once stood around every farm in the Mittelland. Much of the fruit was made into spirits. In the 1930s the state started to tax fruit spirits and had to buy the surplus. Alcohol abuse was also a concern.

From 1950 to 1975 the federal alcohol administration and the cantons organised campaigns to fell fruit trees ('Fällaktionen'). Farmers were asked to replace old tall trees with smaller trees in modern orchards. Machines also work better without scattered trees. The canton of Lucerne counted about 1.3 million fruit trees in 1951 and 330,000 in 2001.

The sample area is the field 'Böler' near Roggwil in Thurgau. The map of 1955 shows fruit trees on the whole field. The map of 1990 still shows many trees. Today's map shows only a few. Since 1993 farmers get federal payments for tall fruit trees, but the number is still falling.
gained: Less surplus fruit spirits. The federal government had to buy the surplus at a fixed price, according to the Zurich farmers’ association.
Fields without scattered trees are easier to work with machines.
lost: About 15 million tall fruit trees in 1950, about 2.2 million in 2023. In Graubünden almost 300,000 trees in 1951, 40,000–50,000 in 1999.
Habitats for birds such as the redstart, wryneck, green woodpecker and hoopoe, and for insects. The farm landscape of the Mittelland lost one of its typical elements.
Between 1985 and 2018 the land statistics counted a loss of 257 km² (35 %) of orchard, vineyard and horticulture area together.

title: Mormont limestone quarry
place: Mormont hill between Eclépens and La Sarraz, north of Lausanne
built: since 1953 (cement works); quarry enlarged step by step until today
summary: Since 1953 a quarry has cut into the wooded Mormont hill to feed the Eclépens cement works; since 2025 a cantonal law forbids any further extension.
why: Cement is made from limestone and clay. In 1953 a cement works was built at the foot of the Mormont hill at Eclépens. Its quarry takes limestone from the hill. The canton says the quarry has played a key role in the cement supply of Switzerland since the 1950s.

The quarry grew step by step with new permits. The map of 1965 shows only a small pit at the east end of the hill. By 1985 about one third of today's quarry was dug. The hill is in the federal inventory of landscapes of national importance (BLN/IFP, object 1023). According to the group 'Sauvons le Mormont', it was listed in 1998. The federal object sheet says the quarry area is an enclave left out of the protected site. In 2006 test trenches for a new quarry stage found a site of the Helvetii (a Celtic people). It dates from about 100 BC and has more than 200 pits.

Several groups went to court against the extension to La Birette. The canton says this extension lies fully outside the protected area. From October 2020 to 30 March 2021 protesters occupied land and buildings of Holcim on the hill, against the extension. EPFL calls this 'ZAD' (zone to defend, a protest occupation) the first in Switzerland. The police cleared it. Since 1 June 2025 a cantonal law forbids any extension of the quarry beyond the areas already allowed. On 28 September 2025 Vaud voters refused the initiative 'Sauvons le Mormont' and accepted the counter-proposal of the authorities.
gained: Limestone for cement close to the works. The canton says the quarry supplies an important part of the country with cement.
The digging led to the discovery and rescue excavation of an important Iron Age site of the Helvetii.
lost: Part of the wooded hilltop is gone. On the swisstopo map of 1965, forest and meadows covered the place where the quarry is today (seen on the maps).
According to the federal inventory sheet, the large quarry and the cement works change the landscape considerably and form an artificial edge of the protected site.

title: Spreitenbach: from farming village to new town
place: Spreitenbach in the Limmat valley, between Dietikon and Killwangen
summary: In the 1960s a 'new Spreitenbach' of high-rise flats and the first Swiss shopping centre grew on the fields of a farming village; the population rose from 1,173 (1950) to 5,978 (1970).
why: In 1950 Spreitenbach was a village of 1,173 people. The Zurich region grew fast after the war and needed homes. With the building of a high-rise in 1955, a building boom started. In 1960 the commune approved a building law with a zoning plan. It planned a 'Neu-Spreitenbach' (new Spreitenbach) on the Langäcker fields, away from the old village.

The high-rise quarter Langäcker was built from 1961 to about 1970 on fields of local farmers. The tallest tower has 26 floors. In 1970 the first shopping centre of Switzerland opened here, on the model of American shopping malls. A second one followed in 1974. The A1 motorway opened in 1971, and the SBB built the Limmattal marshalling yard (1967–1978) on a former gliding field.
By 1970 Spreitenbach had 5,978 people, and 9,127 in 2000. In the 1970s the quarter became a symbol of the critics of modern town planning.
gained: Many new homes. The population grew from 1,173 in 1950 to 9,127 in 2000, and Spreitenbach had 7,186 jobs in 2005.
The first shopping centre of Switzerland (1970), the A1 motorway (1971) and the Limmattal marshalling yard (1967–1978) came to Spreitenbach.
lost: The open fields of the Langäcker and Mitterzelg between the village and the Limmat. In the sample box the village core of 1950 covered about 12 hectares; today the built-up area is about 168 hectares (measured on the maps, method see notes).

A small, still rural commune became a suburb. According to the cantonal heritage office, 'Spreitenbach' soon stood for building that many people saw as wrong. A school wall chart of 1975 used it as a negative example of unchecked urban growth.

title: Gravel pits of the Rafzerfeld
place: Rafzerfeld between Wil, Hüntwangen and Rafz, north of the Rhine near Eglisau
summary: Since the 1960s large pits have taken gravel out of the flat Rafzerfeld; each pit is later filled with clean excavated soil and given back to farming, while new pits open next to it.
why: Concrete for houses, roads and tunnels needs gravel. The canton of Zurich uses about 4 million cubic metres of aggregate (gravel and sand) per year; about 75 % comes from gravel pits. About 80 % of the transport of gravel and excavated soil goes through the large pits of the Zürcher Unterland. Switzerland has about 600 gravel pits.

The Rafzerfeld lies on a very large gravel deposit left by the Ice Age. After 1960 large-scale digging started in the flat fields between Wil and the railway. Two Ice Age slopes once divided the area into an upper and a lower Rafzerfeld; the digging removed most of them. Since 1993 the canton has guided the digging with plans that fix the order of digging, refilling and rail transport.

A pit does not stay open for ever. When the gravel is gone, the pit is filled with clean excavated soil from building sites and farmed again. The map of 1990 shows a pit at Röggliacker; today that land is mostly fields again, with a pond. New pits have opened beside it.
gained: Gravel for the building industry of the canton, close to the users and partly carried by rail.
Some old pits became ponds and nature protection areas. A plan of 2021 foresees up to 133 hectares given back to farming and 26 hectares of near-natural habitats.
lost: The natural relief: the Ice Age slopes between the upper and lower Rafzerfeld are mostly gone.
Until a pit is filled again, the land cannot be farmed. About 80 % of the transport of gravel and excavated soil in the canton goes through the large pits of the Zürcher Unterland.

title: Forest grows on abandoned alpine pastures (since 1985)
place: All of Switzerland, mainly the Alps and the south side of the Alps above about 700–800 m
summary: From 1985 to 2018 about 977 km2 of new forest and woody areas grew in Switzerland, mostly on unproductive land and abandoned alpine pastures.
why: In the mountains many alpine pastures and meadows are steep and give little income. Where farmers stop using them, bushes and trees grow back by themselves. This happens almost only in the mountain areas.

The federal land use statistics (Arealstatistik) compares aerial photos. From 1985 to 2018 it found 977 km2 of new forest and woody areas (before clearings are subtracted). 52% grew on unproductive land, 29% on alpine pastures, 17% on other farmland and 3% on settlement areas.

In the canton of Uri, for example, forest area grew by about 12% from 1985 to 2018, but only above 700 m. New growth that counts as forest may not be grazed or cleared without a permit. To keep pastures, Uri now sets fixed forest borders and allows farmers to clear young growth on alpine pastures.
gained: From 2009 to 2018 alone, forest and woody areas grew by 206 km2 and now cover just under one third of Switzerland.

Forest protects against natural hazards. A summary of WSL research says that species numbers often rise for some time after farming stops. Even if farming disappeared completely, hardly any species would be lost.
lost: Alpine pastures lose fodder. In Uri, three quarters of the regrowth on farmland happens on alpine pastures and in the steepest mountain zones.
Plant and animal communities that depend on farming disappear. During the change from pasture to forest, the risk of erosion and avalanches can rise for some time.
In a national survey, people rated a wooded landscape higher than an open one, but a lightly wooded landscape higher than a heavily wooded one.
